prompt: The electron micrograph (Figure 1) shows an organelle with visible internal stacks of membranes (grana/thylakoids). This organelle is the ___.
hint: The stacked membrane structures (grana/thylakoids) are characteristic of a chloroplast.

prompt: The chloroplast's internal stacks of grana/thylakoid membranes increase the ___ available for light absorption, which drives photosynthesis.
hint: More membrane surface area means more pigment molecules can be packed in to capture light.

prompt: The electron micrograph (Figure 2) shows a small, rod-shaped cell about 2 μm long with no visible membrane-bound nucleus. Is this a prokaryotic or eukaryotic cell?
options: Prokaryotic — it lacks a membrane-bound nucleus and other internal organelles, and is small in size and simple in shape.
Eukaryotic — it has a clearly defined, membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic — because it is small enough to be a red blood cell.
Prokaryotic — because it contains mitochondria.
answer: Prokaryotic — it lacks a membrane-bound nucleus and other internal organelles, and is small in size and simple in shape.
hint: No visible nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, plus a small simple size, points to a prokaryotic cell (e.g. a bacterium).

prompt: In a coastal food web, crabs and Mulberry whelks both eat limpets, while crabs also eat sea urchins. If people increasingly remove larger sea urchins, what is the likely impact on the Mulberry Whelk population?
options: The Mulberry Whelk population would likely decrease, as crabs (losing a food source) compete more for the same limpets that whelks rely on.
The Mulberry Whelk population would increase rapidly with no negative effects.
The Mulberry Whelk population would be completely unaffected, since whelks don't share any food source with crabs.
The Mulberry Whelk population would immediately go extinct.
answer: The Mulberry Whelk population would likely decrease, as crabs (losing a food source) compete more for the same limpets that whelks rely on.
hint: Removing sea urchins pushes crabs toward limpets, increasing competition with whelks for that same food source.

prompt: People selectively removing only the larger sea urchins from a rock platform (leaving smaller ones in crevices) is an example of a human-induced selection pressure. How could this affect the sea urchin population over time?
options: Over time, smaller sea urchins that reach maturity and reproduce at a smaller size may become more common in the population.
The sea urchin population's average size would increase over time.
This pressure has no effect on the genetic makeup of the population.
All sea urchins would evolve to move faster to escape collection.
answer: Over time, smaller sea urchins that reach maturity and reproduce at a smaller size may become more common in the population.
hint: Consistently removing the larger individuals favours the survival and reproduction of smaller ones.

prompt: A red blood cell has a biconcave (dimpled disc) shape with a smooth surface. How does this structure relate to its function of transporting oxygen?
options: The biconcave shape increases surface area to volume ratio (boosting oxygen-carrying capacity) and lets the cell squeeze through narrow blood vessels.
The biconcave shape allows the cell to photosynthesise more efficiently.
The biconcave shape lets the cell divide more rapidly than other cells.
The biconcave shape prevents the cell from ever entering small capillaries.
answer: The biconcave shape increases surface area to volume ratio (boosting oxygen-carrying capacity) and lets the cell squeeze through narrow blood vessels.
hint: Red blood cells are specialised for oxygen transport — their shape maximises surface area and flexibility.

prompt: Why is cell specialisation essential to the survival of multicellular organisms?
options: Multicellular organisms need many different cell types, each specialised for a particular function, so the cells can work together to keep the whole organism alive.
Specialisation allows every cell to perform every function equally well.
Specialisation only matters in unicellular organisms.
Specialised cells no longer need to cooperate with other cells.
answer: Multicellular organisms need many different cell types, each specialised for a particular function, so the cells can work together to keep the whole organism alive.
hint: A multicellular body relies on division of labour between different specialised cell types.

prompt: Which statement best explains how evolutionary change occurs by natural selection, using antibiotic resistance in bacteria as an example?
options: Some bacteria randomly have mutations giving antibiotic resistance; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce more than others when antibiotics are applied, so resistance genes become more common over generations.
All bacteria develop resistance simultaneously as soon as an antibiotic is introduced.
Bacteria consciously choose to become resistant to survive.
Antibiotics directly cause resistance mutations to appear.
answer: Some bacteria randomly have mutations giving antibiotic resistance; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce more than others when antibiotics are applied, so resistance genes become more common over generations.
hint: Natural selection acts on existing variation — the mutation doesn't appear because of the antibiotic, but survival is determined by it.

prompt: Match each substance to the name of the process that transports it through a plant.
hint: Transpiration describes water movement through the plant and its loss from leaves; translocation describes sugar transport in phloem.

prompt: Order the steps that draw water up through the xylem to the leaves, from first to last.
items: Water is pulled up the stem as it evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), held together by cohesion
Water enters root hair cells by osmosis
Water moves cell-to-cell down a concentration gradient into the xylem
answer: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis
Water moves cell-to-cell down a concentration gradient into the xylem
Water is pulled up the stem as it evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), held together by cohesion
hint: This is the transpiration-cohesion-tension mechanism: evaporation at the leaves pulls a continuous column of water up from the roots.

prompt: Phloem, the tissue used to transport sugars from the leaves to other parts of a plant, consists of columns of living cells connected end-to-end through small holes called ___.
hint: Unlike xylem (dead, hollow cells), phloem is made of living cells connected via sieve plates.

prompt: Five 10cm × 10cm quadrats (100cm² each, 500cm² total) were placed on a rock platform and a total of 20 sea urchins were counted. The population density of sea urchins is ___ sea urchins per cm².
Why are ecologists sometimes unable to get actual (complete) counts of certain organisms when collecting population data?
options: Some organisms move too quickly to count accurately, there may be far too many individuals to count (e.g. grass), and complete counts can be too time-consuming and costly.
It is always faster and cheaper to count every single individual than to sample.
Ecologists are legally forbidden from counting all organisms.
All organisms are equally easy to count regardless of size or mobility.
answer: Some organisms move too quickly to count accurately, there may be far too many individuals to count (e.g. grass), and complete counts can be too time-consuming and costly.
hint: This is exactly why sampling techniques like quadrats are used instead of a full census.

prompt: Four cube-shaped shapes have side lengths of 1, 2, 1×1×2 and 1×2×2 units. The shape with the largest surface area to volume ratio is the ___.
hint: For the 1×1×1 cube: surface area = 6, volume = 1, so SA:V = 6:1 — the best ratio of all four shapes.

prompt: Cells are almost always microscopic because smaller cells have a greater ___, letting them exchange nutrients and wastes with their environment more efficiently.
hint: As a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area, making exchange less efficient.

prompt: A diagram shows that chicken, pig, monkey and human embryos look nearly identical in early development — all starting as a fertilised egg, showing similar cell division and body structures (including a tail-like structure). How does this support the theory of evolution?
options: The similarities suggest these organisms share a common ancestor and have gradually evolved different traits since diverging.
The similarities prove these organisms are all the same species.
Embryonic similarities have no connection to evolutionary relationships.
The similarities only prove that all embryos are the same size.
answer: The similarities suggest these organisms share a common ancestor and have gradually evolved different traits since diverging.
hint: Comparative embryology is a classic line of evidence for common ancestry — shared early development points to a shared evolutionary origin.

prompt: In the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane, water can pass through relatively easily, but larger molecules like glucose and charged ions cannot pass through directly. Why?
options: Water is small and can slip between the phospholipids, while larger molecules and ions are blocked by the hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails in the centre of the bilayer, and must instead cross via protein channels.
Water cannot cross the membrane at all, while glucose crosses freely.
The membrane has no effect on which molecules can pass through.
Ions are small enough to easily pass straight through the hydrophobic core, just like water.
answer: Water is small and can slip between the phospholipids, while larger molecules and ions are blocked by the hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails in the centre of the bilayer, and must instead cross via protein channels.
hint: The hydrophobic core of the bilayer blocks larger or charged particles, which need dedicated protein channels to cross.
